newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity seen opening lower in correction.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity seen opening lower in correction.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were expected to open lower Friday in a retracement from large gains Thursday and through much of this week, industry sources said.
"We've had a huge move to the upside and now we're seeing a bit of a correction," said one New York-based futures trader.
In early over the counter discussion, July Palo Verde (PV) was pegged at $33.00-33.60 from a Thursday NYMEX July futures settlement at $35.70 per megawatt hour (MWh), the sources said.
July California Oregon Border (COB) was talked at near $20.50 early Friday from Thursday's NYMEX futures close at $22.23 per MWh.
In Thursday's ACCESS session, July PV was offered at $35.25 and bid at $35.00, while July COB was offered at $24.50 and bid at $21.50 per MWh.
NYMEX PV futures settled sharply higher Thursday after hitting new contract highs on the news of the generation outages in the U.S. West, hot weather in the Southwest and stronger natural gas prices.

COB futures also closed stronger on news of California outages and the PV strength. So far this week, July PV has gained $8.02 per MWh, up 29 percent from last Friday, and July COB has gained $4.43, or 25 percent.
The rise in futures follows a handful of unplanned shutdowns at several fossil-fired plants in California and the Southwest.

PV prices were also given bullish news when Southern California Edison Co pushed back the restart of the 1,080 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 3 nuclear unit in San Clemente, Calif., to July 10 from late June for additional work.
Although the futures were called to open lower, sources said the retrenchment may not last the day, with fundamentals continuing bullish.
"We're seeing some pretty good support at these (early Friday) levels and we're starting to get some buying interest," the New York trader said.
In outage news, the 750 MW unit 5 at the Four Corners, New Mexico, coal-fired plant may be shut for a week after it tripped off-line Wednesday due to a tube rupture,

Several units which were shut for unexpected maintenance were scheduled to return to service soon, including the 750 MW unit 1 at the Mohave coal-fired power plant in Nevada, and two 750 MW units at the Moss Landing natural gas-fired power plant near Monterey, Calif..
The 1,112 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state was tentatively set to restart next Wednesday or Thursday, pending approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

The bullish tone on power futures was also underpinned by a Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) committee plan to derate the Pacific Intertie transmission system from July 1-30 to 6,300 MW from the current limit of 7,200 MW.
The plan still requires the approval of the WSCC board.
Higher air-conditioning demand in the West also has pushed up the region's natural gas prices.
However, traders said electricity prices in the Southwest were sharply lower Friday morning in anticipation of the full return of El Paso Natural Gas Co's Blanco gas plant in the San Juan Basin.

On Friday and Saturday, 240 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas will still be cut, but on Sunday operations at the plant will return to normal. The Blanco plant normally processes about one billion cubic feet per day of gas.
July NYMEX Henry Hub natural gas futures were trading up 1.4 cents at $2.235 per million British thermal units as of 1010 EDT.

Temperatures through the Pacific Northwest were expected to average near to four degrees Fahreneheit below normal through the weekend, then were expected to moderate to near-normal levels early next week. Unsettled weather was seen through the weekend before conditions were forecast to improve early next week.
In the southwest, the weekend and early next week were expected to be mostly dry and hot with temperatures called to be one to six degrees above normal.
((--Chris Reese, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1627))
